Description: A clay foundation cylinder inscription of Nabonidus, king of Babylon (r. 556–539 BC), recording his restoration of three temples: Ehulhul, the temple of the moon-god Sin at Harran; Ebabbar, the temple of the sun-god Shamash at Sippar; and Eulmash, the temple of the goddess Anunitu at Sippar-Anunitu. For each temple Nabonidus claims to have cleared away earlier, faulty work and rebuilt on its original foundation deposit — for Ebabbar, the deposit of Naram-Sin, son of Sargon, which he says no earlier king had found. The text also presents the Persian king Cyrus as the instrument of the god Marduk in defeating the Medes, clearing the way for the rebuilding at Harran. It is a different text from the Nabonidus cylinders from Ur: it contains no prayer for Belshazzar.
Interpretations: Scholars generally date this undated text to after Nabonidus's thirteenth regnal year (543 BC), perhaps his sixteenth year (c. 540 BC); it survives in numerous copies found at both Sippar and Babylon, including copies now in Berlin, London, Istanbul and New York, so it should not be described as a single object with a single findspot. As a royal building inscription it is direct evidence for Nabonidus's reign and temple-building programme, but only contextual background for the biblical account: it does not mention Belshazzar, Daniel, or the fall of Babylon, and its presentation of Cyrus as Marduk's instrument is Nabonidus's own royal theology, not the biblical claim that Cyrus acted at the LORD's command. No single 1881 discovery by Hormuzd Rassam at Sippar for this particular text was verified in the scholarly edition consulted, so DateDiscovered is left blank rather than repeating that claim.
AlternativeNames: Ehulhul Cylinder; Nabonidus Inscription 15; Nabonidus Cylinder III, 2
RelatedEvents: Cyrus's Decree and Return from Exile
BiblicalSignificance: The cylinder sets the historical scene for the closing chapters of the Babylonian empire in Daniel: Nabonidus was the last king of Babylon, and his reign ended with Cyrus's conquest, after which Cyrus permitted the exiles to return, as recorded in Ezra 1 and foreshadowed in Isaiah's naming of Cyrus. It therefore illuminates the world of Daniel 5 and of the return from exile without itself confirming any biblical episode. Readers should note the contrast in framing: Nabonidus credits Marduk with raising up Cyrus, while the Bible credits the LORD.
ArtifactDate: c. 540 BC (undated; after Nabonidus's 13th regnal year)
CurrentLocation: Multiple copies: Vorderasiatisches Museum, Berlin; British Museum, London; and other collections
DiscoveryLocation: Sippar and Babylon (copies found at both sites)
